transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-04-10 15:00 UTC | Duration: 60 minutes | Zoom call
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Cho (Redwood SE), Jared Morales (CortiTech CTO), Priya Singh (ML Eng), Maya Chen (Security)
Shared: deck: https://redwood.app/deck/guardrails (shared), security pack link: https://redwood.app/security-pack, perf spreadsheet: https://redwood.app/benchmarks/CRM-4582

Summary: Technical deep dive focused on safety/moderation placement and the perf overheads. Customer wants guidance on where to place filters (pre/inline/post), how that interacts with batching/KV cache/quantization, and tradeoffs for hosted vs dedicated vs on-prem VPC.

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros, i'm Samir, AE on this deal, lena's our se.
[00:18] Lena: Hi all, i'll walk through the perf implications and some recommended patterns.
[00:32] Jared: Thanks, we've been seeing higher tail latency when we run moderation inline. curious about tradeoffs.
[00:45] Priya: Our target p95 is 350ms for short prompts (<=512 tokens). We get decent throughput but moderation seems to double latency in-host.
[01:02] Maya: From security, we need deterministic blocking for high-risk content and audit logs. can't rely on purely async post-hoc checks for some flows.

[02:10] Lena: good context. to frame things, there are 3 common placement options for safety/moderation: pre-filter (client-side or edge), inline (during generation or as additional scoring step), and post-filter (async or synchronous after generation). each has perf and correctness tradeoffs.
[02:40] Speaker 1: (mumbled) also there's hybrid patterns...
[03:00] Lena: yes, hybrid is often best: lightweight classifier at the edge to block obvious stuff, then heavier multi-modal moderation async or in a fallback path.

[04:12] Samir: i'll add how this interacts with caching: if you do pre-filter before request hits the runtime, you avoid wasting model cycles, but you also reduce caching opportunities because the request might be rejected before it would produce a cached response. conversely, post-filter after generation allows you to cache model outputs, but you risk caching content that later needs to be removed.
[04:40] Priya: so caching is dangerous if moderation runs after caching, right?
[04:48] Lena: yep. best practice: if you plan to cache outputs (prefix or full response), ensure the moderation decision is determinative for cacheability. in practice teams do: (a) run a lightweight safety check pre-cache to decide if response should be allowed into cache, (b) store responses with metadata and a TTL and revalidate when policy changes.

[06:05] Jared: what about inline moderation during generation—token level checks? we heard about that from another vendor.
[06:18] Lena: token-level (or incremental) moderation is possible; you can run classifiers on partial outputs. the upside is you never generate or send disallowed text; downside is additional compute per token and it interferes with batching and KV cache locality. incremental checks can kill batching benefits because they require per-request synchronization points. also some token checks add per-token latency of plus 1-3ms depending on classifier size.
[06:55] Priya: is that 1-3ms per token or per check?
[07:01] Lena: per classifier inference. so if you run a lightweight model on logits for every generated token it compounds. for a 100 token response that could be 100x the classifier latency unless you batch classifier calls. but batching classifier calls is complex because generation is length-varying.

[08:30] Maya: we need auditable decisions. would running moderation as a separate synchronous call be acceptable? e.g. generate -> moderation sync -> return to user.
[08:45] Lena: that's the post-filter sync pattern. it's simple, keeps model runtime simple, and can be parallelized to a moderation cluster. it's easier to scale independently and to leverage different models. the downside is additional end-to-end latency (model latency + moderation latency). you can mitigate with async UX—return partial or safe placeholders while heavy checks run.

[10:00] Samir: quantitative estimates we typically see in our benchmarks: a medium-weight moderation classifier (distil-BERT-like) adds ~25-80ms if run as a single inference per request; token-level classification adds marginal ms per token and can blow up. note these numbers vary by hardware. on our dedicated infra GPUs, you can run moderate-sized classifiers faster, but inference GPU occupancy for generative model dominates cost.
[10:38] Jared: and how does quantization affect classifier speed?
[10:44] Lena: quantization helps both the generator and the classifier. int8/4-bit quant on the generator reduces per-token latency and memory, allowing higher throughput so the relative overhead of a classifier shrinks. however quantization can slightly change logits distribution; if you rely on subtle scoring thresholds for safety, you should validate.

[12:05] Priya: KV cache question: if we use KV cache for prefix caching across similar sessions, does moderation need to check on every invocation?
[12:18] Lena: depends: KV cache stores internal states, prefix caching stores the model outputs for identical prefixes. if a response was previously cached and you trust the prior moderation state, you can serve cached content quickly. but if policies changed or you discovered a false negative, cached items should be invalidated. typical pattern: tag cached entries with moderation version/tags and invalidate on policy changes.
[12:45] Speaker 2: (background) cache eviction...

[13:10] Lena: batching interactions: our runtime does continuous batching to improve GPU utilization. moderation inserted synchronously at model runtime breaks batching unless the moderation call is batched as well. For hosted API we can co-batch moderation checks on CPU or smaller GPUs; on private deployments you need to architect a separate moderation service that can accept batched inputs.
[13:45] Samir: this is why we recommend separating concerns: keep the generator pipeline as batch-friendly as possible; run lightweight filters at edge to keep bad traffic out; heavy checks can be async or batched separately.

[15:00] Jared: customer constraints: we run in a VPC with strict egress policies and want on-prem for PHI. how does this change patterns?
[15:15] Lena: on-prem/VPC: you can colocate moderator service inside the same network so calls are low-latency. the main difference is resource planning: you need capacity for both generator and moderation if moderation runs sync. for dedicated we can provision co-located GPUs/CPU instances with autoscale policies. for on-prem you might prefer CPU-based lightweight classifiers plus occasional GPU at peak.
[15:50] Maya: audit logs and KMS: we need tamper-evident logs for moderation decisions and keys for model artifacts.
[16:00] Samir: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and audit log exports. we'll share the SOC2 and design notes.

[18:20] Priya: any numbers for cost impact? if we double-check every request with a classifier that's extra compute cost.
[18:33] Lena: rough heuristic: a synchronous classifier per request can add 10-40% to cost depending on classifier size and traffic patterns. If you can push checks to be pre-filter edge CPU (cheap), you can keep added cost <5%. Async increases operational cost but not perceived latency. Exact numbers depend on batch sizes, model size and hardware.

[20:10] Jared: does Redwood support model-level policy tags / moderation versions so we can rotate classifiers?
[20:20] Lena: yes — we have metadata tagging for model outputs and a moderation versioning scheme in the runtime. cached outputs include policy_version so you can invalidate by tag.

[22:00] Samir: let's talk about graceful degradation: if moderation service is down, what's recommended?
[22:08] Lena: fallback options: (1) fail closed — block generation (safe but degraded UX), (2) fail open with lightweight heuristics (riskier), (3) fall back to a more restrictive model variant or canned responses. most regulated customers choose fail-closed or canned fallback with an alerting pipeline.

[24:10] Priya: what about model-specific mitigations like built-in safe decoding or constrained decoding?
[24:20] Lena: constrained decoding (bad words lists, token banning) is cheap and fast; put it in-line in the generator, it's just constrained logits post-processing. this is a great first-line guard because it has negligible compute cost and doesn't break batching. combine that with pre-filter and async checks.

[26:30] Jared: ok for our initial pilot we want: inline constrained decoding + edge lightweight filter + asynchronous heavy moderation and audit logs. acceptable?
[26:42] Maya: yes that meets security posture if audit logs are comprehensive.

[28:00] Lena: operational notes: when you run asynchronous moderation, include correlation ids so you can tie a generation to moderation decision. also store moderation verdicts and the classifier version used. this helps for forensics and ML drift analysis.

[30:15] Samir: specific perf numbers we'll aim to collect in the pilot: p50/p95/p99 latency for generation alone, end-to-end latency with inline constraints, end-to-end with sync moderation, and throughput with KV cache warm and cold. also classifier latency and cost per 10k requests. Lena will run the benchmark with your prompts.

[31:00] Priya: one more question—does batching the generator with KV cache warmup affect latency spikes? we see occasional bursts.
[31:12] Lena: yes, warmup helps a lot. if KV cache is cold you pay for cache fill; continuous batching improves throughput but can increase tail latency if you wait to accumulate batch. our runtime has latency-aware batching to bound tail. in dedicated pools you can tune batching thresholds to meet SLOs.

[33:00] Jared: any gotchas with quantization plus constrained decoding?
[33:08] Lena: quantization is mostly orthogonal to constrained decoding. the main gotcha is verifying that your constrained tokens are handled correctly by the quantized kernels—some older kernels had token id mapping quirks. we validate per-model. also quantization may slightly change generation probabilities so if you have strict threshold-based heuristics you should validate with test prompts.

[35:10] Speaker 3: (background) license...

[36:00] Maya: compliance question: if we keep moderation offline async, can we still meet regulatory obligations for real-time blocking?
[36:12] Lena: it depends on the regulation. for PII or PHI flows often you need synchronous blocking. our recommendation: synchronous blocking for regulated paths, async for lower-risk experiences. you can route by policy: high-risk paths go to sync pipeline with stricter controls.

[38:00] Jared: how do we measure classification drift and monitor quality of the moderator?
[38:12] Lena: we instrument false positive/negative metrics, sample outputs periodically for human review, and run continuous evals (holdout sets). Redwood Optimize can run scheduled evals and alert on regression; we'll show you the dashboard in the follow-up.

[40:30] Priya: any suggestions for initial classifier architecture? lightweight distil transformer on CPU for edge, larger transformer on GPU for heavy checks?
[40:42] Lena: that's the usual pattern. lightweight binary classifier at edge (fast, low compute), heavier multi-class/moderation ensemble on GPU for flagged cases. ensemble outputs feed into policy engine.

[42:50] Samir: we should also discuss costs for dedicated vs hosted for this usage: dedicated gives predictable latency and colocated moderations, but requires commit; hosted gives easier autoscaling but you pay for moderation egress and maybe higher per-request costs.
[43:12] Jared: we prefer dedicated if latency tails are better.

[45:00] Lena: we can include a config we call "safety placement profiles": starter, enterprise, strict. starter = edge lightweight + constrained decoding. enterprise = + async heavy moderation and tagging. strict = sync heavy moderation for regulated paths. We'll include recommended autoscale knobs and batching thresholds per profile.

[47:00] Maya: please capture sequence diagrams for the flow.
[47:10] Samir: will do, we'll attach to the follow-up email.

[49:20] Priya: note that some of our prompts are long (2k tokens) — how does that affect overhead?
[49:30] Lena: long context increases generator cost linearly, KV cache helps when there's repetition. moderation cost depends on whether you run checks over entire output or context + output; for long contexts you may pre-scan input client-side to remove PII before sending. that reduces both model and moderation load.

[52:00] Jared: final recap?
[52:10] Samir: recap: recommended pilot: constrained decoding inline, edge pre-filter lightweight classifier, async heavy moderation with audit logs, KV cache with policy-tagged entries, quantize generator for cost savings but validate moderation thresholds, dedicated pilot recommended for lowest tail latencies. next steps: samir send security + pricing, lena run bench, customer provide prompts.
[52:45] Maya: we'll expect the SOC2 and design notes.
[53:10] Priya: we'll upload prompts by tomorrow.
[53:30] Samir: great, thanks everyone. we'll follow up with calendar invite for the benchmark review.
[54:00] (call ends)
